newsitem.title: USA: N.J. approves pension bonds, now faces court fight.
newsitem.headline: N.J. approves pension bonds, now faces court fight.

text.p: - It took hours of wheedling to get a majority for Gov. Christie Whitman's $2.8 billion pension bond issue through the the state Senate Thursday night, but it faces a new challenge today.

A Superior Court judge Friday plans to hear a constitutional challenge to the plan to borrow the money to liquidate state unfunded pension obligations by selling bonds. It also helps balance the next budget.
Whitman signed the bill into law late last night.

The Senate began its voting session late in the afternoon with the issue still unresolved. The Republican majority resumed deliberations in caucus at 1800 EDT, after voting for other bills on the agenda.

A solid block of Democratic opposition joined by five or six Republican senators had stymied the proposal, which would enable the administration to avoid $590 million in pension payments through June 1998.

In the wake of a warning from Standard & Poors Corp., several senators said they could not vote for a bill that endangered the state's credit rating. Earlier this week, S&P softened its statement, but did not move the opposition.

Some lawmakers argued that the savings generated by the deal was not needed, since tax revenues are coming in far above budget projections, giving the administration a cushion it estimates to be more than $200 million. The respected Office of Legislative Services puts the number at $494 million, and others say even that number is conservative.

There was strong sentiment within the Republican majority to wait until closer to the June 30 deadline for passing a balanced budget. Whitman proposed a $16.2 billion spending plan for the fiscal year starting July 1.
"There is a date certain by which we have to pass the bond issue or find an alternative route to a balanced budget, but June 5th is not that date," said state Sen. Joseph Kyrillos, R- Middlesex.

The governor's chief counsel, Michael Torpey, lobbied for action Thursday. He pointed out that the state was due to make a $200 million pension payment within days, and once paid it cannot be recovered. A previous administration had drawn IRS scrutiny of a pension maneuver that enabled it to recover monies already paid into the four funds.
Whitman said last week her plan is needed to provide about $250 million to achieve the level of state aid the state Supreme Court ordered May 14 for 28 poor school districts.

Whitman's original pension bond plan was to borrow $3.4 billion, enabling her to forgo $647 million in contributions to the state's four funds. The state Senate pared it and reduced its budget benefit to $590 million.
New Jersey has already selected Merrill Lynch & Co to underwrite the bond deal.
